title.rendered: “He had his whole life ahead of him”; Company fined after 21-year-old tyre fitter killed when truck fell on him at roadside

content.rendered:
• Niall Fawcett died when he was struck by a truck while he was working beneath it on the M56 slip road in Cheshire.
  • HSE found the company failed to properly assess risks of replacing a blown-out tyre on a low-profile truck.
  • Victim was not adequately supervised or monitored despite only holding roadside licence for less than four months.

A commercial tyre service provider in Worcestershire has been fined following the death of 21-year-old employee Niall Fawcett, who was killed while carrying out a roadside repair.

On 2 August 2024, Mr Fawcett was called out to replace a blown-out tyre on a low-profile truck on the slip road at junction 7 of the M56 motorway near Bowdon. While he was positioned beneath the truck, it is understood to have slipped from the bottle jack (a compact hydraulic lifting tool designed for vehicle support) being used to raise the vehicle and landed on him, causing fatal head injuries.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Halford Commercial Fleet Services Limited, formerly known as Lodge Tyre Company Limited (The), had not properly assessed the risks associated with replacing a blown-out tyre on a low-profile vehicle. The company had also failed to give employees suitable work instructions, including information on when a truck should be recovered rather than repaired at the roadside.

The investigation also found that Mr Fawcett had only obtained his licence to work on commercial tyres at the roadside when he joined the company less than four months before his death. Despite this, he had not been subject to any monitoring or supervision to ensure that he was working safely.

The HSE publication Health and safety in motor vehicle repair and associated industries sets out the importance of providing safe systems of work and ensuring workers are competent to carry out their tasks.

The impact on Niall’s family

Niall’s mother, Sharon, said in her victim personal statement:

“Niall was only 21 years old when he died. He had his whole life ahead of him. He was planning to marry the following year and he and Megan were saving for a deposit on their first home together and talking about starting a family. Niall was building for a life he was excited for and this was taken from him in an instant.

“Niall went to work that day and should have been safe, supported and protected. Instead, my son never came home.”

Halford Commercial Fleet Services Limited, of Icknield Street Drive, Washford West, Redditch, Worcestershire B98 0DE, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £600,000 and ordered to pay a victim surcharge of £200 and £24,203 in costs at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 3 November 2026.

HSE Principal Inspector Laura Royales said:

“This case should serve to highlight to employers the importance of properly assessing the risks to which their workers are exposed and providing the right information and instructions, supplemented by adequate monitoring and supervision arrangements, to ensure that they can and do work safely.

Our thoughts remain with Niall’s family as they continue to come to terms with their tragic loss.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Matthew Reynolds and paralegal officer Benjamin Stobbart. The investigation was supported by Visiting Officer Natty Heath.

 

Further information:

  1. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
  2. More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
  3. Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
  4. Relevant guidance can be found here Health and safety in motor vehicle repair and associated industries
  5. HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.  The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found here.

title.rendered: Ministry of Defence issued with Crown Censure over death of soldier during Salisbury Plain exercise

content.rendered:
• Private Jethro Watson-Pickering was killed during an exercise on Salisbury Plain
  • 23-year-old died from head injuries after gun barrel of his armoured vehicle struck a tree on 15 October 2021
  • MOD issued with Crown Censure by Health and Safety Executive

The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has been issued with a Crown Censure by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) after a British Army soldier died during a routine training exercise on Salisbury Plain.

The censure follows an investigation by HSE inspectors into the incident in 2021, which concluded the MoD had not met its duties under the Health and Safety at Work Act, and found inadequacies with the risk assessment, instructions and training for the exercise.

The incident

Private Jethro Watson-Pickering, of the 1st Battalion of the Yorkshire Regiment, was taking part in an exercise known as Iron Storm at the British Army’s Salisbury Plain training area in Wiltshire on 15 October 2021. The 23-year-old had been driving a Scimitar-variant Combat Vehicle Reconnaissance (Tracked) (CVR(T)) armoured fighting vehicle. Their role in the exercise was to drive armoured vehicles and act as the enemy for another Army regiment.

At around 11:50am the incident vehicle was escaping ‘attack’, when the gun barrel, protruding beyond the side of the vehicle, struck a tree. On impact, the turret rotated very quickly, and the rear storage bin attached to the it struck Private Watson-Pickering’s head, causing fatal injuries. He died at the scene.

HSE investigation

An investigation by the HSE found there was no safe system of work for driving the CVR(T) Scimitar during the exercise.

Risk assessments failed to identify the danger to the driver from the turret rotating without warning. As a result, no control measures were put in place to stop the driver’s head being struck by a storage box if the barrel was accidentally hit and the turret turned.

The investigation also found that risk assessments were not properly reviewed after similar incidents in previous years. Instruction and training were also inadequate, particularly on the risk of the turret rotating unintentionally and on driving with the head up.

Crown Censure

Following the investigation, a file was passed to HSE’s legal services division, which concluded there was sufficient evidence to pursue a Crown Censure.

A Crown Censure is the maximum sanction available to HSE against a Crown body. It acts as an official reprimand and provides a lasting, public record of a Crown body’s failure to comply with the law.

By accepting the Crown Censure, the MoD admitted breaching its duty under Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.

HSE inspector Emma O’Hara said:

“Our thoughts are first and foremost with the family and friends of Private Jethro Watson-Pickering, who must live with his loss.

“Just like any other employer, the MOD has a responsibility to take all reasonably practicable steps to control the risks to the safety of its employees. In this case, it failed to do so, which has cost a young man his life.

“While realistic exercises are an essential component of military training, this does not mean employees should face uncontrolled or inadequately controlled risks.

“Training exercises must be properly planned, with risks identified and mitigated, to prevent future tragic incidents like this one.”

The HSE Crown Censure was brought by HSE enforcement lawyers Rebecca Schwartz and Tom Ledden-Rocks, and paralegal officer Helen Jacob.

 

Further information:

  1. The Health and safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety.
  2. The breach of law the Censure is being issued over is: Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, which states that: “It shall be the duty of every employer to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all his employees”.
  3. There is no financial penalty associated with Crown Censure, but once accepted is an official record of a failing to meet the standards set out in law.
  4. Crown Censure is the process by which HSE holds Crown bodies to account for serious breaches of health and safety law. You can find a record of Crown Censures issued by HSE at: Crown Censures taken by HSE since 1 April 1999.

title.rendered: Independent review recommends continued rodenticide stewardship under strengthened regime

content.rendered:
An independent government oversight review has found that the UK’s stewardship regime for professional rodenticide use has delivered important safeguards for human health, animal health and the environment, and should continue but with strengthened monitoring and support for users. 

The review was carried out by the UK Rodenticide Stewardship Government Oversight Group (GOG), a cross-government body chaired by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) on behalf of its members. HSE is publishing the review’s findings on behalf of GOG. 

The GOG review found that the stewardship approach has delivered clear benefits. It has put in place effective governance of the supply chain, ensuring professional rodenticide products are only sold through approved outlets to trained users operating as part of an integrated pest management strategy. It has also built a more competent workforce, improving users’ understanding of, and approach to, rodent control, and established consistent monitoring that allows the environmental impacts of rodenticide use to be measured and assessed. 

Importantly, the review also found that stewardship has not yet delivered a measurable reduction in total second generation anticoagulant rodenticide residues in barn owls compared with the pre-stewardship baseline, meaning a key performance measure has not been met. The GOG review is clear that this finding does not mean risk has gone unmitigated and does not represent an overall failure of stewardship. Without the steps already taken to improve workforce competence and restrict access to trained, competent users, GOG’s view is that the risks to human health, animal health and the environment would likely be greater than they are today. 

GOG has recommended that stewardship, and the Campaign for Responsible Rodenticide Use UK (CRRU UK) regime, should continue, but be strengthened. Additional measures include extending environmental monitoring, funding new analysis of residues, developing further insight into key user groups, and improving how information is delivered to users. 

Richard Daniels, Director of Chemicals Regulation Division at HSE said: 

“Anticoagulant rodenticides are powerful tools, which would not normally be approved. They are only authorised for use because they are essential to protect human health, animal health and the environment from the serious risks posed by rodent infestations. That is precisely why it’s so important that they are used responsibly. 

“This independent review reports that stewardship is working in putting significant safeguards in place, ensuring these products reach only trained, competent users who understand how to use them safely and effectively.  

“HSE will now consider the Oversight Group’s report and recommendations in strengthening the scheme further, for example through better monitoring and support for those who use these products when it considers, alongside other information, whether rodenticides should continue to be authorised for use.” 

Ends 

Notes to editors 

  1. The UK Rodenticide Stewardship Government Oversight Group (GOG) is an independent, cross-government body. HSE chairs the group and is publishing this report on its behalf. 
  2. The Campaign for Responsible Rodenticide Use UK (CRRU UK) is an industry-led stewardship scheme introduced in 2016. 
  3. Anticoagulant rodenticides are among the most effective tools available for controlling rats and mice, but their toxicity means they do not meet the normal criteria for authorisation under biocides legislation. They are permitted only because the active substances they contain have been assessed as essential to prevent serious danger to human health, animal health and the environment, and because not authorising them would cause disproportionate harm to society compared with the risks of their use. This conclusion was reached by the European Commission in 2017 and remains the basis for their continued availability. 
  4. In 2016, industry introduced the Campaign for Responsible Rodenticide Use UK (CRRU UK) stewardship regime to minimise exposure and the risk to people, animals and the environment, restricting supply of professional products to trained, competent users and requiring ongoing environmental monitoring. 
  5. At the time, government and industry agreed the scheme would be reviewed after 5 years to assess whether it was delivering its intended benefits, including a measurable reduction in rodenticide residues found in barn owls, used as a sentinel species for wider environmental exposure. 
  6. HSE is currently carrying out routine renewal assessments of anticoagulant rodenticide products. The conclusions and recommendations of the GOG report will be taken into account as part of this decision-making process.  
  7. Government Oversight Group report is available here.

title.rendered: HSE takes action to strengthen asbestos safety standards following consultation

content.rendered:
The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) has today published its response to a consultation on proposals to strengthen the regulatory framework for managing asbestos.

The consultation sought views on three proposals regarding the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 (CAR 2012), all aimed at reducing exposure to legacy asbestos, which remains a  risk in Great Britain due to its use in construction before being banned in 1999.

The responses have led to HSE making a regulatory change to strengthen independence and impartiality in the four-stage clearance process. HSE will amend regulation 20 of CAR 2012, which covers standards for air testing and site clearance certification, to remove the potential conflicts of interest that may arise when the LARC appoints the asbestos analyst.

Later this year, HSE will update the Approved Code of Practice (L143) Managing and working with asbestos – HSE and Asbestos: The Analysts’ Guide – HSE, and has developed simple online guidance to help dutyholders appoint third-party service providers with confidence. Industry will have 12 months to comply with the changes.

In addition, HSE continues to strongly recommend that dutyholders use accredited organisations when commissioning asbestos surveys and is developing further guidance and interventions to help dutyholders understand the critical role a quality survey plays in managing asbestos risk safely.

Finally, the consultation has resulted in the category of work known as Notifiable Non-Licensed Work (NNLW) being retained. HSE will work collaboratively with industry to develop improved guidance to support the correct use of this category.

Across all three proposals, responses consistently pointed to behaviours and competence, particularly around dutyholder understanding of their responsibilities under the regulations, commissioning practices, and the practical application of regulatory requirements. This evidence will be used to inform the design of further interventions and guidance.

Rick Brunt, Director of Engagement and Policy at HSE, said:

“Thanks to those who responded, we gathered substantial evidence helping us to develop a greater understanding of the issues that underlined each of the proposals and to help support policy development and decision-making.

“We are now able to confidently strengthen asbestos safety regulations and make changes to guidance that will help us deliver on our commitment to reduce asbestos exposure across Great Britain.”

Minister for Social Security and Disability, Sir Stephen Timms, said:

“The dangers of exposure to asbestos are well known. Its terrible legacy from its use in the past remains a risk for many people in the present.

“To protect people in Britain, we have a mature and well-established approach to the management of asbestos in buildings.

“Today we are strengthening this protection to improve the safety of our workers and the public from asbestos exposure.”

The publication of the consultation response follows the laying of a Statutory Instrument in parliament to amend the regulations which will come into force on 24 November 2026, with industry having a year to comply before HSE enforces the change in November 2027.

HSE will continue to monitor and evaluate the effectiveness of these changes once implemented. The outcomes in response to the consultation represent the delivery of the three outstanding recommendations made by the 2022 Work and Pensions report on the HSE’s approach to asbestos management accepted by the previous Government.

 Notes to editors

  • The consultation, “Legislative and guidance proposals for the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012”, ran from 10 Nov 2025 to 9 Jan 2026 and received 358 responses.
  • The consultation looked at three separate proposals:
  1. Proposal to  ensure the independence and impartiality of roles in the four-stage clearance process
  2. Proposal to improve the quality of asbestos surveys
  3. Proposal to clarify the type of work that constitutes work with asbestos known as Notifiable Non-Licensed Work (NNLW)
  • The full consultation response is available at Legislative and guidance proposals for the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 – Health and Safety Executive – Citizen Space
  • The Statutory Instrument will come into force on 24 November 2026 and is subject to parliamentary procedure.

title.rendered: HSE urges employers to take action on work-related stress during Stress Awareness Week

content.rendered:
• Work-related stress remains one of the leading causes of work-related ill health in Great Britain
  • HSE is encouraging employers and managers to take practical action during Stress Awareness Week through its Working Minds campaign
  • Free tools, guidance and resources are available to help employers identify and address the causes of stress

As Stress Awareness Week begins, the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is encouraging employers and managers to take practical action to prevent and manage work-related stress.

Work-related stress remains one of the leading causes of work-related ill health in Great Britain. Left unaddressed, it can affect workers’ health and wellbeing, increase sickness absence and impact workplace performance.

The good news is that small actions can make a big difference. Whether it’s starting a conversation, reviewing workplace pressures or making use of available support, every workplace can take steps to reduce stress and support good mental health.

Many employers still do not realise that they must assess and manage the risks of work-related stress in the same way as other workplace health and safety risks. Identifying the causes of stress, assessing who may be affected and taking action to eliminate or control risks are important steps in protecting workers’ health and preventing harm.

Through its Working Minds campaign, HSE is encouraging employers and managers to take action using the 5Rs approach:

Reach Out – Start conversations about stress and mental wellbeing.

Recognise – Understand the signs and causes of stress.

Respond – Take action to address concerns and support workers.

Reflect – Review what is working and where improvements can be made.

Make it Routine – Embed good practice into everyday working life.

HSE is also highlighting its Management Standards approach, which helps employers identify and address six key areas of work that can contribute to stress if they are not managed effectively:

  • Demands
  • Control
  • Support
  • Relationships
  • Role
  • Change

By understanding these factors, engaging with workers and assessing associated risks, organisations can identify potential issues and take action before they affect health and productivity.

Kayleigh Roberts, HSE’s Work-Related Stress Policy Lead, said:

“Work-related stress is a health and safety issue. Employers should assess the risks of stress, and its impact on mental and physical ill-health, in the same way they assess other work-related health and safety risks.

By understanding the causes of stress, engaging with workers and taking action to eliminate or control risks, employers can help create workplaces where people feel supported, valued and able to perform at their best.

Stress Awareness Week is a valuable opportunity for employers and managers to review what they are doing, start conversations with workers and take practical steps to prevent work-related stress.”

HSE’s Working Minds campaign provides a range of free tools, guidance and resources, including the Talking Toolkit, Stress Indicator Tool, online learning modules and downloadable guidance materials.

During Stress Awareness Week, employers should:

  • If necessary, review their stress risk assessment and ensure it reflects current workplace risks, identifying where further action may be needed to eliminate or control those risks.
  • Use the Talking Toolkit to have structured conversations with workers.
  • Discuss the six Management Standards areas with their teams.
  • Encourage managers to access Working Minds training and resources.
  • Consider how the 5Rs can be embedded into everyday workplace practices.

While Stress Awareness Week provides a valuable focus, preventing and managing work-related stress should remain a priority throughout the year. Regular conversations, meaningful engagement with workers, effective risk assessment and action to eliminate or control workplace risks can help build healthier, more productive and more resilient workplaces.

For free tools, guidance and resources, visit the Working Minds campaign.

 

Further information:

  1. Employers have a legal duty to assess and manage risks to workers’ health, including risks to mental health.
  2. The Working Minds campaign provides free resources, including the Talking Toolkit, Stress Indicator Tool, Management Standards guidance and online learning modules.
  3. Stress Awareness Week takes place from 2-6 November 2026.
  4. For interview requests, case studies or further information, contact the HSE Press Office at enquiries@hse.gov.uk.

title.rendered: PICTURED: Aftermath of apartment roof blaze workers ‘lucky to escape’ from

content.rendered:
• Photos taken after fire on roof of apartment block show damage
  • Four workers forced to flee blaze with just one ladder as their escape route
  • No fire extinguishers, no means of raising the alarm and no permit for welding work
  • C Watkins Plumbing Limited fined after HSE investigation finds company failed to follow its own hot works procedures

Shocking photographs taken in the aftermath of a fire on the roof of an apartment block in Surrey show how lucky four workers were to escape.

A contractor has been fined after the workers had to flee a fire that engulfed the roof of a 14-storey apartment building under construction in Surrey.

The four subcontractors were working under the control of C Watkins Plumbing Limited, installing an air source heat pump on the roof of the Old Telephone Exchange development in Staines-upon-Thames, when the incident happened on 26 June 2024.

Sparks from welding work ignited uncovered rigid foam insulation that had been laid across the roof. The self-sustaining fire developed quickly, spreading across the whole of the roof space before burning itself out when it ran out of fuel.

The men escaped through a single opening in the floor and down a ladder to Level 14. There was no other way off the roof, no means of raising the alarm, and no fire extinguishers.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company had failed to plan, manage and monitor the hot works on the roof. Despite the company having policies requiring them, there was no risk assessment or method statement in place, and a permit to work was not issued for the welding.

HSE’s guidance, HSG168 – Fire Safety in Construction, states that fire safety measures must be considered throughout all stages of design and procurement, and implemented effectively during construction. It says risk assessments must identify high-risk activities where fires can spread quickly, and situations where evacuation plans are complex, and that all risk assessments and control measures must be reviewed throughout the construction phase to make sure they remain suitable and sufficient.

C Watkins Plumbing Limited, of Watkins House, Leigh Road, Haine Industrial Park, Ramsgate, Kent, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 15(2) of the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £8,270 in costs at Staines Magistrates’ Court on 29 October 2026.

HSE inspector Stephanie Hickford-Smith said:

“Watkins failed to follow its own procedures for hot works. It did not assess the risks and so had no control measures in place.

“The four men working on the roof were lucky to escape. Had the fire started closer to their escape route, or had they not acted as quickly as they did, the outcome could have been devastatingly different.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE senior enforcement lawyers James Towey and Laura Lax and paralegal officer Farhat Basir.

 

Further information:

  1. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
  2. More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
  3. Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
  4. HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.  The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences in Scotland can be found here.

title.rendered: “This accident took away my freedom”; Vehicle recovery company fined after worker crushed under truck left unable to walk unaided

content.rendered:
• Simon Pedder was crushed under a reversing recovery truck and now needs crutches, a frame and a wheelchair.
  • More than 10 months on, he has been unable to return to work and says, “life will never be the same”.
  • HSE found the company had no suitable traffic management system and no adequate precautions for reversing vehicles – which remain a leading cause of workplace injury.

A Swindon-based vehicle recovery business has been fined after a worker was struck by a reversing vehicle and suffered life-changing injuries.

On 13 June 2025, Simon Pedder was undertaking yard duties at Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited in Highworth when he was suddenly hit and crushed under a company-owned recovery truck.

Mr Pedder suffered fractures to both legs and an arm, a punctured lung and a fractured rib. He was airlifted to the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, where he spent five weeks and underwent several operations to rebuild his legs, including skin grafts.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited had failed to implement a suitable traffic management system to make sure vehicles and pedestrians could circulate safely and had not implemented proper precautions to assist reversing drivers.

(Photographs showing before and after HSE intervention)

More than 10 months later, Mr Pedder’s recovery has not progressed as he had hoped. The extent of his injuries means that in addition to using crutches, a Zimmer frame and wheelchair, Simon now needs regular care visits and cannot carry out basic tasks like getting into the shower without help. He has been told he will most likely need walking aids for the rest of his life.

Describing the impact of the incident on his life, Mr Pedder said:

“I used to be a very sociable person, the life of the party, both in work and with friends; this has been taken away from me as now I spend my days sitting at home by myself. My mood is very low, and this is affecting not only myself but also my family, who say my personality appears to have changed completely.”

He added, “there are many basic things I can’t do, for example, I can’t cut the grass, I can’t fold the washing, I can’t go for a walk, and I am not allowed to drive. This accident took away my freedom.”

He also described the impact on his family, with his wife cutting short her working hours to support his care, and the family rearranging the living room to accommodate a hospital bed. Mr Pedder said: “I feel so bad because I am affecting those who are close to me. My life will never be the same and I feel like this accident should never have happened as I was only doing my job.”

Failure to manage reversing vehicle risks

HSE inspectors found failures by Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited to properly control the risk of reversing vehicles – despite this being one of the leading causes of workplace fatal injury. To manage workplace transport effectively, employers should consider the risks associated with their site and vehicles. Where workers are required to operate on foot in areas where there are moving vehicles, employers must ensure traffic routes are organised in a way that prevents collisions between pedestrians and vehicles.

HSE guidance advises implementing a one-way system for vehicle circulation to eliminate the need for reversing. Where this isn’t possible, the site should be organised to include safety measures such as protective barriers, clear markings and pedestrian crossing points. To aid a driver’s field of vision and alert pedestrians to reversing vehicles, precautionary measures such as rear-view cameras and warning alarms should also be fitted to vehicles.

Guidance on workplace transport safety is freely available on the HSE website: Workplace transport – HSE.

Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited, based at Blackworth Industrial Estate, Highworth, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £28,000 and ordered to pay £7,276 in costs at Bristol Magistrates’ Court on 29 October 2026.

HSE Inspector Laura Artosi said:

“Almost 25 per cent of fatal workplace transport accidents in Great Britain occur while a vehicle is reversing – a stark reminder to employers to properly assess and manage this fundamental risk.

“Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited lacked a suitable traffic management system, including adequate arrangements to ensure vehicles could reverse without risks to those on foot. These failings led to an incident that has robbed Simon Pedder of much of his freedom and will likely have a lasting impact on his life.

“Had Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited implemented robust measures to allow pedestrians and vehicles to move safely across its site, this incident would not have occurred.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Karen Park and paralegal officer Michael Millman.

Further information:

  1. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
  2. More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
  3. Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
  4. Relevant guidance can be found here: A guide to workplace transport safety – HSE and Safe manoeuvring – HSE.
  5. HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.  The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found here: Health and safety offences, corporate manslaughter and food safety and hygiene offences

title.rendered: Fish processing firm fined almost a quarter of a million pounds after worker’s arm pulled into machine after safety guard left off

content.rendered:
• Worker suffered fractured jaw and chest and arm trauma when he was pulled into a conveyor mechanism
  • A section of fixed guarding had been removed two weeks earlier and not replaced
  • Company’s guarding checks did not include non-electrical fixed guards

A Peterhead fish processing company has been fined £245,000 after a worker was dragged into a machine through a gap where a safety guard should have been.

The man, then aged 30, was working as a chargehand on a production line at Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage Company Limited’s premises in Peterhead on 19 August 2025 when the incident happened.

What happened

The worker had stopped to deal with a box that had jammed too high in a rack loader cage to be reached from the ground. He entered the production line through a gap in the guarding without isolating the power, then climbed onto the conveyor and pressed down on the lid to release the jam. The machine restarted, and his right arm was pulled into the pusher section of the rack loader. Unable to free himself, he was drawn further into the mechanism until his head made contact with moving parts.

A colleague who heard the worker’s shouts for help isolated the power and stopped the machine. The man was taken to Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, where he was found to have a fractured jaw and trauma to his chest and right arm. He needed surgery to insert metal plates in his jaw and spent three days in hospital. He returned to work on 29 September 2025 and has made a full recovery.

HSE investigation

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that a section of fixed guarding next to the production line had been removed during maintenance around two weeks before the incident and had not been put back. Without the guard, the gap gave access to the machine without the power being isolated. The correct route in, through an interlocked gate, would have switched off the machinery as soon as the gate was opened.

HSE found that, while the guard was missing, staff had used the gap to reach the machinery on various occasions when boxes jammed, rather than the interlocked gate. Maintenance staff told HSE they had seen the guard missing and had seen employees using the gap, but it was not reinstated. The weekly inspection checklist used by the in-house maintenance team did not include checking the integrity of non-electrical fixed guarding.

Had the guarding been in place, the only way into the machine would have been through the interlocked gate, and the incident would not have happened.

HSE guidance highlights the importance of following safe isolation and lock-off procedures before any maintenance or cleaning work is carried out. Employers must ensure all machinery is properly isolated from power sources, and that systems are regularly monitored and reviewed to prevent inadvertent start-up. Further guidance is available here: The safe isolation of plant and equipment – HSE.

Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage Company Ltd, of East Quay, The Harbour, Peterhead, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) and (2) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 and Section 33(1)(c) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £245,000 and ordered to pay a with a victim surcharge of £18,375, at Peterhead Sheriff Court on 28 October 2026.

HSE inspector Nicky Smith said:

“This was a wholly preventable incident which left a worker seriously injured.

“A missing guard and an unchecked gap left the way open for a worker to be dragged into a machine.

“Guards must be kept in place, and checks must cover every guard, not just the electrical ones.”

 

Further information:

  1. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
  2. More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
  3. Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
  4. HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so.  The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences in Scotland can be found here.

title.rendered: Engineering company fined after worker suffers finger amputation

content.rendered:
• Worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded saw.
  • HSE investigation found the company had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous moving parts.
  • Company fined after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998.

An engineering company has been fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation after a worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded automatic saw.

Thomas Davies, 21, was working for Dlinexsign Ltd when the incident occurred. Having reached into the machine to retrieve a cut piece of material, his hand came into contact with the moving saw blade, resulting in him losing part of his finger.

The incident occurred at the company’s premises at Buckingham Road Industrial Estate, Brackley. The machine was used to cut lengths of material, and Mr Davies was able to reach into the machine and access the dangerous moving parts while it was operating.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Dlinexsign Ltd had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to the dangerous parts of the machinery.

HSE guidance states that employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery. This will normally be achieved using fixed guarding, but where access is required, other protective measures such as interlocked guards may be necessary to ensure dangerous movement has stopped before a person can reach the danger zone.

Further guidance can be found on HSE’s website on the safe use of work equipment: Introduction to machinery safety – HSE.

Dlinexsign Ltd, of Shires Road, Brackley, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation to Mr Davies, and £9,064.34 in prosecution costs at Milton Keynes Magistrates’ Court on 23 October 2026.

HSE Inspector Dulanjala Kandana-Arachchige said:
“This incident demonstrates the serious consequences that can result when access to dangerous parts of machinery is not effectively prevented.

“Employers must ensure that machinery is properly guarded and that effective measures are in place to prevent workers from reaching dangerous moving parts.

“This was a preventable incident. Employers have a responsibility to ensure that work equipment can be used safely and that workers are protected from dangerous machinery.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Tom Ledden-Rocks and paralegal officer Natalie Ellis.

title.rendered: Company fined for providing false electrical safety certificates for car washes

content.rendered:
• Two car wash companies in Runcorn found to be unsafe and ordered to stop work
  • Company hired to carry out repairs issued false certificates declaring they were safe
  • Sites continuing operating despite electrocution risks to workers and members of the public

A company has been fined after it falsely supplied electrical safety certificates to two car wash businesses in Runcorn, despite them both being declared unsafe.

Inspectors from Britain’s workplace regulator – alongside colleagues from Cheshire Police, Trading Standards and the immigration authorities – carried out an investigation into the activities of Super Hand Car Wash on Halton Road and Top Star Hand Car Wash on Bridge Street.

Both premises were found to have electrical systems that were dangerous. This resulted in Health and Safety Executive (HSE) inspectors taking enforcement action against both businesses – forcing them to immediately stop work. The car wash owners were advised to use a National Inspection Council for Electrical Installation Contracting (NICEIC) registered electrical contractor or similar, to ensure that electrics were made safe to ensure the safety of the public and the people working on site.

Epco Energy Solutions Limited, who were at the time, members of the NICEIC were engaged to carry out the work and certified the installations as being safe to use.

However, an examination of the certificates by one of HSE’s specialist electrical inspectors found that details in them did not match the installations he found on site.  A subsequent visit to both car washes found that the installations were still dangerous and presented a risk of serious injury or electrocution to those on site, including members of the public.

The Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require all electrical installations to be maintained in a safe condition. This means that systems should only be worked on by someone who is a competent electrical contractor.  The NICEIC is one of the certification bodies for electrical contractors in the UK.  Membership of such a body indicates that the member has received appropriate training, and has been assessed to ensure that they are competent to carry out work on electrical systems. HSE guidance on electrical safety is available. Electrical safety – HSE

Epco Energy Solutions Limited had visited and provided electronically generated certificates using the NICEIC secure members only systems. Certificates provided to the car washes indicated that the electrical systems on site were safe to use when they were not.  With support from the NICEIC it was found that the certificates had been generated using password protected software and electronically signed with sole Epco Director Mohammed Naeem’s signature.

Epco Energy Solutions Limited, of Unit B, 37 Worlsey Road, Eccles, Manchester, were found guilty after a trial at Warrington Magistrates Court on 2 September 2026, of breaching section 3(1) of the Health and Safety At Work Act 1974 etc, 1974. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £15,239 at the same court on 22 October 2026.

HSE inspector Rose Leese-Weller said:

“Due to having such a close relationship with water, car wash owners must ensure that their electrical installations are maintained in a safe condition.

“As well as being safe to use they must also be fit for purpose so as to prevent serious personal injury or electrocution to anyone in the vicinity.

“These car washes where dangerous and unsafe – to both those working there and to members of the public visiting the sites.

“Electrical installations at all workplaces must be maintained in a safe condition and are safe to use.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by enforcement lawyer Sam Crockett and paralegal officer Hettie Burrows.

title.rendered: Fine for manufacturing company after man left as ‘a shadow of his former self’

content.rendered:
• Gary Taylor, suffered multiple injuries when he was hit on the head by a one- tonne metal hopper
  • He spent three weeks in hospital and had to take seven months off work
  • E H Hassell & Sons Limited fined £300,000 for failing to properly plan for work

A Staffordshire-based manufacturing company has been fined £300,000 after a family man was left with injuries so serious he became ‘a shadow of his former self’.

Gary Taylor, who was 63 at the time, spent three weeks in hospital and needed seven months off work, following the incident on 24 March 2025.

The grandfather had been working for E H Hassell & Sons Limited at its site on Newstead Ind Estate in Trentham. He was one of several workers involved in the unloading of a lorry trailer containing various steel components for a large filtration system.

The workers had improvised a system to unload the metal hopper with a forklift truck, placing the forks underneath the unsecured load to lift it from the trailer bed. However, as it slid from the forks, it struck Mr Taylor in the head as he was stood alongside it. His injuries included fractures to his skull, neck and spine, two broken ribs and a severe laceration to his forehead which required 17 staples and 14 stitches.

Mr Taylor described how the incident has had a lasting impact on his life.

“During my time off recuperating from my injuries, the seven months I was off work, I had no interest in anything,” he said.

“I know my wife thinks that I won’t be around with her in my eighties, she has constant worry that something is going to happen to me.

“She never thought like that before my accident.

“For me, I have no idea what the future holds.

“I can only hope that I will get better as time goes on and I become more like the old man I used to be – a supportive husband, father and grandfather to my grandchildren.

“I want to be a person that hopefully will become more of a person than a shadow of my former self.”

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the lifting operation had not been properly planned by a competent person. The characteristics of the load, including its weight, size, centre of gravity and lifting points, had not been adequately assessed, and no safe system of work had been put in place.

Moving an object of this size and weight was not a regular task at the site and there was no established system of work for it.

HSE guidance on Planning and organising lifting operations – HSE states that it is important to properly resource, plan and organise lifting operations so they are carried out in a safe manner.

E H Hassell & Sons Limited of Alderflat Drive, Trentham, Staffordshire pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 8(1) of the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 and were fined £300,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,690 at a hearing at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court on 23 October 2026.

HSE inspector Claire Whitehurst said:

“The failures here resulted in an experienced worker suffering life-changing injuries.

“The company failed to properly plan the lifting operation or implement a safe system of work.

“Mr Taylor suffered serious injuries which could easily have resulted in his death. He has been left with facial scarring, and both he and his family have been deeply affected by this traumatic experience.

“Employers must ensure that lifting operations are properly planned by a competent person and carried out safely. This is especially important for non-routine tasks involving heavy or awkward loads.”

The HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer, Julian White and supported by HSE paralegal officer, Stephen Grabe. The investigation was supported by visiting officer, Natalka Heath.

title.rendered: Bed springs company fined after worker injured in warehouse collision

content.rendered:
• CCTV captures moment a ride-on pallet truck collides with fork lift truck inside busy warehouse in Barnsley
  • 20-year-old worker suffered several fractures to his foot and nerve damage
  • Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited had failed to consider impact of changes it had made to workplace transport routes

CCTV has captured the moment a young worker was injured when the ride-on pallet truck he was using collided with a fork lift truck in a warehouse in Yorkshire.

Bed spring manufacturer Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited has been fined after Charlie O’Dowd was injured in the incident at its Long Royd warehouse in Barnsley on 14 November 2024.

The then 20-year-old had been using a ride-on pallet truck during the installation of new automated machinery within the warehouse. However, his truck, which was unguarded, collided with a fork lift truck being driven by another employee, resulting in multiple fractures to his foot, as well as longer term nerve damage.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company had made changes to its workplace transport routes to accommodate the installation works taking place. However, these changes meant that both ride-on pallet trucks and fork lift trucks were required to use the same routes, within what was a busy stock loading area. Visibility was limited and vehicle movements had increased.

The HSE investigation concluded that the company had focused on the installation of the new machinery but had failed to adequately consider the impact that significant changes to workplace transport arrangements would have on worker safety. The changes to vehicle routes had not been properly risk assessed before being implemented.

Every year, there are accidents involving transport in the workplace, some of which result in people being killed. HSE guidance explains what should be done to keep workers safe – Introduction to workplace transport safety – HSE.

Leggett & Platt Components Europe Limited, pleaded guilty to a breach of  Section 2(1) of the Health & Safey at Work etc. Act 1974 in relation to the safe use of workplace transport within the warehouse. The company was fined £80,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £3,374 at Leeds Magistrates Court on 20 October 2026.

HSE Inspector Chris Parker said:

“This case highlights the importance of carefully assessing the wider safety implications of any changes made within a workplace, even where those changes may be temporary.

“When workplace transport routes are altered, employers must ensure that the risks created by those changes are properly assessed and controlled before they are introduced.

“Had suitable planning and risk assessment been carried out, this incident could have been prevented.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Julian White and paralegal officer Zara Salman and advocacy undertaken by enforcement lawyer Arfaq Nabi.

title.rendered: Half-a-million pound fine for company after worker suffers 40 per cent burns

content.rendered:
• Three-tonne steel beam fell into bath of molten zinc that created wave that covered worker
  • 33-year-old man spent 11 days in intensive care requiring 13 operations
  • Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited fined more than £500k after HSE investigation finds chains used to lift beam were damaged and deteriorated

One of Britain’s leading steel galvanizers has been fined more than £500,000 after one of its workers suffered 40 per cent burns to his body when hit by a wave of molten zinc at its site in Devon.

The employee was working for Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited at its site in Marsh End, Lords Meadow Industrial Estate in Crediton, Mid Devon, when the incident happened on 12 October 2021.

Hot dip galvanizing is a process that provides long-term protection against rust and corrosion of steel products. On the day in question, a lifting chain, carrying a roller steel joist weighing nearly three tonnes, failed. The beam fell into a galvanizing bath and the resulting wave of molten zinc covered the 33-year-old, before hitting a wall and surging back along the floor towards him.

CCTV footage from the scene shows the worker alight and running towards the emergency shower where his clothes were removed and he was doused in water. He was initially treated at the scene by paramedics, before being taken by air ambulance to Southmead hospital in Bristol. He had suffered 40 per cent burns and remained in intensive care for 11 days undergoing 13 separate operations. Any remaining healthy skin was grafted to repair his burnt body.

During his lengthy treatment the man suffered infection and sepsis leaving him with multiple long-term health conditions.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the set of chains used to lift the heavy steel beam had signs of damage and deterioration and there was a failure to withdraw them. Crucially, the chains had not undergone their mandatory regular inspection.

The investigation also revealed that the load slinging arrangement used at the time of the incident was incorrect, which meant that the load being lifted was greater than the safe limit for the chains. The risk assessment in place at the time of the incident for “immersion & swilling” had no reference to checks on chains, or what type of sling configuration to use.

Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited failed to meet several regulations and standards. Under the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations (LOLER) 1998, lifting accessories must be thoroughly examined by a competent person at least every six months. Both the Lifting Equipment Engineers Association (LEEA) code of practice and the user manual for the chain manufacturer state that chain slings used in acidic environments, such as zinc galvanising, should be inspected before each day’s use.

The Health and Safety Executive publishes freely available guidance which underlines the importance of thorough inspection of lifting equipment, including the benefits of an ‘examination scheme’.

Wedge Group Galvanizing Limited of Stafford Street, Willenhall, West Midlands, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 3(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £566,666 and ordered to pay £15,521 in costs at Bristol Magistrates Court on Wednesday 14 October 2026.

HSE inspector Alexander Ashen said:

“This wholly-avoidable incident led to a young man having to endure truly terrible injuries – and the disturbing truth is that the consequences could have been even worse.

“It is shocking that an industry-leading firm,, with considerable resources at its disposal, should risk the lives of its workers with substandard inspection protocols.

“Our thoughts are with the victim at the heart of this incident, his friends and family, and all those at the site who have been affected by what happened that day.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Gemma Zakrzewski, Paralegal Officer, Farhat Basir and Rowena Goodwin, Enforcement Advocate.

title.rendered: CCTV captures terrifying runaway Range Rover incident that left passer-by with life-changing injuries

content.rendered:
• CCTV shows recovery driver being dragged beneath runaway Range Rover on Bournemouth hill
  • Member of the public suffered broken legs and spinal fractures after trying to help
  • HSE investigation found recovery driver failed to secure two-tonne vehicle before it rolled out of control

A vehicle recovery driver has pleaded guilty after a runaway Range Rover he failed to secure rolled down a hill in Bournemouth, dragging him beneath the vehicle before crushing a member of the public who attempted to help.

Sean Baker, a vehicle recovery driver for GRS Recovery Bournemouth, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 following the incident on Exeter Crescent, Bournemouth.

CCTV footage shows Sean Baker being dragged beneath the Range Rover after it suddenly rolled away during a recovery operation on a steep hill.

Nearby, Kai Dransfield was on a break from his job at TGI Fridays when he witnessed the incident unfold.

He saw the Range Rover begin to roll down the hill with Sean Baker trapped beneath it and later described him as “hanging on for dear life”.

Mr Dransfield said:

“He made eye contact with me, and my first thought was to just grab him to try and help him.”

In attempting to help, Mr Dransfield was struck by the vehicle and pulled underneath it.

The Range Rover rolled over both of his legs, causing serious injuries including multiple broken bones in his legs and fractures to his spine.

More than two years later, Mr Dransfield continues to suffer constant pain and has difficulty walking.

HSE found that Sean Baker had initially attached a winch to the front of the Range Rover, which would have prevented the vehicle rolling away if the handbrake was released or failed.

However, he later removed the winch, jacked up the vehicle and placed skates beneath the rear wheels.

The wheels were not secured with chocks and no breakaway cables were attached. As a result, when the vehicle was lowered onto the skates there was nothing in place to prevent it rolling away down the incline.

This resulted in Sean Baker becoming trapped beneath the vehicle and being dragged down the road as it rolled downhill.

The investigation concluded that Sean Baker failed to take reasonable care for his own safety and that of others by not following established recovery procedures. HSE found that his actions fell far below the standard expected of a competent and experienced recovery driver.

HSE guidance states that all risks must be properly assessed and safe systems for working at the roadside prepared. Further guidance can be found here: Essential precautions for working roadside.

Sean Baker pleaded guilty to breaching Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. Sean Baker received 14-week prison sentence, suspended for one year at Bournemouth Crown Court on Friday 16 October 2026.

After the hearing, HSE inspector Alexander Ashen said:

“Sean Baker was an experienced recovery driver. Failing to properly secure a vehicle weighing more than two tonnes on a steep hill was a fundamental error.

“This happened in a busy town centre, close to restaurants and car parks, with vehicles, motorcyclists and pedestrians regularly passing through the area.

“Sean Baker’s failings were substantial, they exposed everyone nearby to risk and resulted in a member of the public, who stepped in to help, suffering life-changing injuries.

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Andrew Siddall and paralegal Officer, Gabrielle O’Sullivan.

title.rendered: Electrical wholesaler fined £4million after worker’s crush injuries mean he now needs 24/7 care

content.rendered:
• 40-year-old father of one was crushed by load weighing over 200kg
  • His injuries were so serious he now lives in a care home
  • City Electrical Factors Limited failed to plan work properly and fined £4million

A Telford-based electrical wholesaler and manufacturer has been fined £4million after an employee sustained life-changing injuries when he was crushed during loading operations using a forklift truck.

The 40-year-old father of one from Telford was working for City Electrical Factors Limited at its Proteus Switchgear Industrial Division on 4 October 2024 when the incident happened.

The man had been acting as a “spotter” while a forklift truck loaded heavy switchboard equipment onto a flatbed lorry. The load, which weighed 231kg, was not secured to the forklift and fell on top of him. He sustained brain and spine injuries and underwent lifesaving surgery. However, he can no longer do anything for himself and is unable to communicate with others. As a result of these injuries, he now lives in a care home and requires 24/7 care.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that City Electrical Factors Limited failed to ensure that the lifting operation was properly planned by a competent person, appropriately supervised and carried out in a safe manner. There was no risk assessment or lift plan, and employees had not been provided with information or instructions about the lifting operation, despite this being a regular activity.

The investigation also found that the load could have been secured to the forklift truck using pre-existing anchor points. The load also had lifting eyes welded to it, which meant that the crane attached to the delivery lorry could have been used as a safer alternative to the forklift truck. Instead, employees were appointed as “spotters” and were expected to steady the loads whilst they were being moved and lifted. This was clearly an unsafe and unnecessary system of work.

HSE guidance states that lift plans should address the risks identified by the risk assessment and identify the resources required, the procedures and the responsibilities so that risks are managed, and any lifting operation is carried out safely. You can read more about our guidance here: Planning and organising lifting operations – HSE.

City Electrical Factors Limited pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £4m and ordered to pay £6,304 in costs at Birmingham Magistrates Court on 16 October 2026.

HSE inspector Keeley Eves said:

“This incident had truly tragic consequences.

“To make matters worse it was completely avoidable and caused by a failure to properly plan for the job taking place.

“The company could have used safer alternative methods to lift the load, such as the lorry-mounted crane which was available, instead of using the forklift truck.

“Instead, the employee was placed at unnecessary risk and now has to live with his devastating injuries.

“Loading and unloading operations remain one of the most hazardous transport activities in the workplace. Employers must ensure that lifting operations are properly planned by competent persons, supervised and carried out safely.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Julian White and paralegal officer Lynne Thomas, while the investigation was supported by visiting officer Sarah Ough.

title.rendered: Fishing fleet company fined following engine room fatality

content.rendered:
• Apprentice engineer Conor Moseley, 20, died when a fire suppression system unexpectedly activated, filling the engine room with toxic gases.
  • HSE investigation found no safe system of work existed for coordinating multiple contractors working in the cramped engine room, and no effective emergency plan was in place.
  • Company fined after pleading guilty to two charges under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.

One of Britain’s leading fishing industry firms has been fined £100,000 after an apprentice engineer died in the engine room of a trawler in Newlyn Harbour.

Conor Moseley, aged 20, died when fire extinguisher gases left him unable to escape the engine room of a trawler on 15 November 2019.

Conor and three other workers were carrying out work on the Resurgam, a fishing vessel owned and operated by W. Stevenson & Sons Limited, when a fire suppression system being installed by Ocean Engineering (Fire) Ltd unexpectedly activated. It filled the engine room with hot, toxic gases, creating dangerous conditions and making it difficult to see.

The small, enclosed engine room had only one way in and out. Workers had to climb a ladder and pass through a hatch one at a time, passing through a gas jet in excess of 75°C. The other workers managed to climb out, but Conor was overcome by carbon monoxide and other substances, leaving him unable to escape.

His colleagues tried to rescue him, putting themselves at risk in the process, but they were unable to reach him. Cornwall Fire and Rescue Service later rescued Conor from the engine room, but he could not be revived.

Tracy Moseley, Conor’s mother, reflected on her son’s life and the impact his death has had on them.

“Growing up Conor loved nothing better than helping out on his dad’s boat.

“Conor always made himself available to help his father when he came in from sea and would be ready to help him land his catch even after a full day’s work. Now for Steve, my husband, there is just an empty place that cannot be filled.

“All we have now are his ashes which are kept in his bedroom.  Every morning I go in and say, ‘morning little man I love you’ and blow him a kiss.  I never say ‘good morning’ as it can never be a good morning without him.

“At night I blow him a kiss and say ‘night night little man, I love you’.”

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the risks created by several contractors working in the cramped engine room had not been properly considered. One contractor described the room as a mess, with poor lighting and trip hazards, and said that at one point six or seven people were working in the space. One witness described it as chaos.

There was no safe system of work for installing the fire suppression system and no effective emergency plan. A permit-to-work system could have been used to coordinate the different activities and ensure they were carried out safely. HSE’s Safety in Docks Approved Code of Practice highlights the need for parties to work together and have an overall written plan covering responsibilities, shared risks and emergency arrangements.

At Truro Crown Court on 15 October 2026, W. Stevenson & Sons Ltd entered guilty pleas to two charges under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, sections 2(1) and 3(1). The company was fined £100,000 and ordered to pay full costs of £27,906.

HSE principal inspector Helena Allum said:

“This was a particularly complicated case requiring significant HSE specialist and scientific input. A number of duty holders played a part in the circumstances leading to the death of Conor; all were investigated.

“While W. Stevenson & Sons Ltd was not responsible for the fire suppression system going off unexpectedly, it was responsible for considering what could go wrong during the installation and maintenance activities, and coordinating them so that as few people as possible were put at risk.

“They had not considered how workers could be quickly rescued in an emergency and receive prompt medical attention. This should be a key consideration when people are working in a restricted space.

“Conor’s death was a tragedy. He need not have been in the engine room at the time. When the worst happened, they couldn’t get him out in time to save him.”

This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE senior enforcement lawyer Jon Mack and paralegal officer Mike Millman.

title.rendered: Media company fined and director sentenced after employee suffers life-changing injuries after filming inside a moving vehicle

content.rendered:
• Company fined £45000
  • Injured person has been unable to return to work
  • No risk assessment had been carried out for the filming activity

A media company has been fined and its director given a suspended custodial sentence after an employee suffered life-changing head and brain injuries when he fell from the back of a moving vehicle during filming in Devon .

The employee was working for Superhub Ltd on 14 May 2021 and was filming a video review of a new electric motorbike at Broadsands car park in Paignton.

After completing the planned filming using a drone, the decision was made to capture additional footage from a moving vehicle, with the motorbike following behind.

The employee climbed into the boot of a car driven by Superhub Ltd director James Foster, and they completed several laps of the car park. As the car began to move the boot liner slipped, causing the employee to fall onto the tarmac.

He sustained serious head and brain injuries requiring long-term care and has been unable to return to work since.

A joint investigation by Devon and Cornwall Police and the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that no risk assessment had been carried out for the filming activity. Investigators also found that the car was unsuitable for the task, as there was no provision to secure the employee or his filming equipment safely while the vehicle was moving.

HSE guidance states that camera operators should not film from footwells, sunroofs, open boots or side doors while a vehicle is moving unless suitable controls are in place to reduce the risk of injury or falling from the vehicle.

The guidance also states that tracking shots involving moving vehicles should only be carried out using suitable vehicles that maintain their structural integrity, with all crew members appropriately restrained.

Superhub Ltd, of Business Hub, Marine Parade, Paignton, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. Director James Foster pleaded guilty to breaching Section 37(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and to causing injury by wanton and furious driving.

Superhub Ltd was fined £45,000 and ordered to pay £3000 in costs. The Judge combined the individual charges and James Foster was sentenced to 16 months imprisonment suspended for 2 years. He was also ordered to pay £2500 in costs at Exeter Crown Court on Wednesday 14 October.

HSE Inspector Emma O’Hara said:

“An employee suffered life-changing injuries as a result of an incident that should never have happened and could easily have been prevented.

“Those responsible for filming activities must properly assess the risks and ensure that suitable equipment and safety measures are in place before work begins. No film, photo, or piece of content is ever worth risking someone’s life. Safety must always come first, and no filming activity should put people in harm’s way.”

“The sentences imposed today should serve as a reminder that HSE will not hesitate to take action against companies and individuals who fail to meet their responsibilities to protect people from harm.”

The HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Rebecca Schwartz and paralegal officer Helen Jacob.

title.rendered: Noise and vibration: HSE warns employers not to wait until the damage is done

content.rendered:
New campaign highlights how employers can prevent permanent hearing loss, tinnitus and hand-arm vibration syndrome through effective workplace action 

  • Around 15,000 workers develop hearing problems caused or made worse by work every year, with an estimated one in five exposed to harmful noise levels. 
  • HSE launches a new campaign during Bone and Joint Health Week, building on its work to reduce HAVS, including the Prevention Programme’s HAVS Risk Reduction Pledge. 
  • Campaign promotes a simple three-step approach – Assess. Control. Protect. – to help employers prevent permanent, life-changing ill health. 

Around 15,000 workers develop hearing problems caused or made worse by work every year, while an estimated one in five workers is exposed to harmful levels of noise at work. 

The effects can be permanent, with workers often unaware they are being harmed until symptoms begin to appear, by which time some damage may already be irreversible. 

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is today launching a new campaign urging employers to assess workplace noise and vibration risks, reduce exposure and protect workers from preventable ill health. 

Launched during Bone and Joint Health Week, and building on HSE’s wider work to reduce Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS), including the Prevention Programme’s HAVS Risk Reduction Pledge, the campaign highlights the importance of taking action before workers’ health is affected. 

Noise and vibration are common workplace hazards across sectors including construction, manufacturing, agriculture, utilities, waste management, engineering, maintenance and entertainment and events. Exposure often comes from tools, machinery and equipment used every day. 

Prolonged or excessive exposure to noise can cause permanent hearing loss and tinnitus. Hand-arm vibration can lead to HAVS and carpal tunnel syndrome, causing numbness, tingling, pain and reduced grip strength. These conditions can affect workers’ ability to do their jobs and carry out everyday activities, sometimes for the rest of their lives. 

Hearing loss can make it difficult to follow conversations with family and friends, while tinnitus can cause persistent ringing or buzzing in the ears, affecting concentration and sleep. For those living with HAVS, everyday tasks such as fastening buttons, holding a cup or using tools can become difficult. 

Chris Steel, Principal Specialist Inspector (Noise and Vibration), said: 

“Noise and vibration-related ill health is preventable, but the consequences can last a lifetime. 

“Workers may not realise they’re being harmed until their hearing is affected, or they begin to experience pain, numbness or tingling in their hands and arms. 

“Employers shouldn’t wait for symptoms to appear. They need to identify where workers are at risk, reduce exposure and make sure the right controls are in place. 

“We’ve already seen organisations demonstrate their commitment to tackling vibration risks through the HAVS Risk Reduction Pledge. This campaign helps employers turn that commitment into practical action. 

“Taking action early can protect workers’ health and prevent conditions that can affect their lives for years to come.” 

Employers have legal duties to assess and control workplace noise and vibration risks under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 and the Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005. 

HSE’s campaign encourages employers to follow three simple steps: 

Assess 

Identify who may be exposed to noise and vibration, understand the risks and carry out suitable and sufficient risk assessments. 

Control 

Reduce exposure at source by choosing quieter or lower-vibration equipment, maintaining tools and machinery, introducing engineering controls and adopting safer ways of working. 

Protect 

Where risks remain, provide suitable hearing protection, arrange health surveillance where required, and give workers the information, instruction and training they need to protect themselves. 

The campaign provides practical tools, guidance and resources to help employers assess workplace risks, put effective controls in place and prevent life-changing occupational ill health. 

The campaign complements HSE’s Prevention Programme to reduce vibration-related ill health, including the HAVS Risk Reduction Pledge. The pledge encourages organisations to commit to reducing vibration-related ill health through effective risk management, worker involvement and long-term prevention. Employers can find out more and sign the pledge at https://www.councilforworkandhealth.org.uk/news/havs-risk-reduction-pledge-get-involved-and-sign-the-pledge/ 

For advice and practical resources, visit HSE’s Noise and Vibration campaign website.

Further information:

  1. Around 15,000 workers experience hearing problems caused or made worse by work each year. 
  2. HSE estimates that around one in five workers is exposed to harmful levels of noise at work. 
  3. Exposure to excessive workplace noise can cause permanent hearing loss and tinnitus. 
  4. Hand-arm vibration can cause Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS) and carpal tunnel syndrome. 
  5. Workers may be exposed to noise and vibration in sectors including construction, manufacturing, agriculture, utilities, waste management, engineering, maintenance and entertainment and events. 
  6. Employers have legal duties under the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 and the Control of Vibration at Work Regulations 2005 to assess and control risks. 
  7. HSE’s campaign promotes a simple approach: Assess. Control. Protect. 
  8. The campaign supports HSE’s Prevention Programme to reduce vibration-related ill health, including the HAVS Risk Reduction Pledge. 
  9. Campaign resources are available through HSE’s Work Right campaign: https://workright.campaign.gov.uk/noise-and-vibration/

title.rendered: Landlord sentenced for leaving gas boiler unchecked for eight years

content.rendered:
• Adam Evans was landlord of property and failed to get safety checks on gas boiler for eight years
  • His tenant was a woman who lived in the property with her five children
  • Annual gas safety checks are a legal duty

A landlord has been sentenced after failing to ensure gas safety checks were carried out at a rented property in Wirral.

An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that property owner Adam Evans failed to have annual safety checks carried out for a period of eight years. The house, on Salisbury Drive in New Ferry, was occupied by a tenant who lived with her five children.

HSE began its investigation in October 2024 after receiving a concern from Wirral Borough Council. The woman had lived at the property since 2016 and reported that no annual gas safety checks had been carried out during her tenancy.

Following enquiries, HSE requested copies of gas safety records from Mr Evans. He provided a certificate dated November 2024 that had been completed following the concern, but was unable to supply any records covering the previous eight years.

Gas safety checks are a basic legal requirement for landlords and are essential to ensure that appliances and flues are safe. Failing to have these checks carried out places tenants at risk of serious harm, including carbon monoxide poisoning.

The sentencing comes after the HSE issued a warning to the public recently amid a surge in prosecutions against those carrying out illegal gas work – Families warned of risk to life from unregistered gas work amid surge in prosecutions of illegal traders – HSE Media Centre.

Adam Evans, of Brownlow Road, New Ferry, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 36(3) of the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998. He was fined £2,400 and ordered to pay £5,000 in costs at Wirral Magistrates’ Court on 8 October 2025.

Members of the public are reminded that landlords must ensure that gas appliances are checked every 12 months by a Gas Safe registered engineer and that records of these checks are retained. Carbon monoxide alarms should also be installed to provide an early warning of danger.

HSE inspector Ian Betley said:

“Adam Evans showed a complete disregard for the law and put the lives of a mother and her children at risk.

“The case highlights a serious failure by him to comply with well-established gas safety requirements.

“Annual gas safety checks are a legal duty and are in place to protect tenants from very real and potentially fatal risks.

“Landlords must ensure that gas appliances and flues are properly maintained and inspected by a Gas Safe registered engineer. Failure to do so will not be tolerated and enforcement action will be taken.”

Gas engineers and consumers can contact the Gas Safe Register in any of these ways:

Website: www.gassaferegister.co.uk

Phone – Consumers: 0800 408 5500; Engineers: 0800 408 5577

Email – enquiries@gassaferegister.co.uk

This prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Chloe Ward and paralegal officer Sarah Thomas.
